title: Review: Using materials (chemistry only); The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.10.4-c02, 4.10.4-c03, 4.10.3-c11, 4.10.3-c12. Clues: 4.10.4-c02 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.10.4-c03 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.10.3-c11 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.10.3-c12 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.10.3-q27, 4.10.4-q07, 4.10.3-q23, 4.10.4-q06, 4.10.3-q26, 4.10.4-q10, 4.10.3-q20, 4.10.4-q04, 4.10.3-q22, 4.10.4-q09, 4.10.3-q24, 4.10.4-q08, 4.10.4-q18, 4.10.4-q19, 4.10.4-q29, 4.10.4-q30. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ammonia
items.clue: The compound NH3 made by the Haber process.

items.label: Raw material
items.clue: A substance fed into an industrial process.

items.label: Bronze
items.clue: An alloy of copper and tin, used for statues, ornaments and bells.

items.label: Brass
items.clue: An alloy of copper and zinc, used for musical instruments, door fittings and taps.

questions.stem: A table gives: aluminium alloy, density 2.7 g/cm3, does not shatter; soda-lime glass, density 2.5 g/cm3, shatters when dropped; carbon fibre composite, density 1.6 g/cm3, does not shatter. Which material is lightest for a given volume and survives being dropped?

options.text: Soda-lime glass, since glass is the lightest here
Aluminium alloy, since a metal can never break
The carbon fibre composite, the least dense
Aluminium alloy, as it is the densest one

questions.stem: The Haber reaction is reversible. What does this mean inside the reactor?

options.text: All the nitrogen and hydrogen react, then some ammonia breaks down
The reaction runs forwards during the day and backwards at night
The ammonia formed can never break down once it is made
Some of the ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen

questions.explanation: The specification states that the reaction is reversible, so some of the ammonia produced breaks down again.

questions.stem: Why do thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated?

options.text: The strong covalent bonds along the chains break
Any solid will melt if it is heated enough
Separate chains are held only by weak forces
The polymer is a liquid that was frozen

questions.explanation: The chains are separate and tangled, with only weak forces between them, so they slide apart when heated.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?

options.text: It increases the yield of ammonia formed at equilibrium
It only speeds up the reaction at 450 degrees C or above
It speeds up the rate at which the equilibrium is reached
It stops the ammonia formed from breaking down again

questions.explanation: The catalyst raises the rate of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner.

questions.stem: Which of these materials is a composite?

options.text: Brass, which is copper mixed with zinc
Concrete, gravel held together by cement
Poly(ethene), made from many ethene units
Soda-lime glass, made by melting sand

questions.explanation: Concrete is a composite: cement is the matrix and the gravel is the reinforcement.

questions.stem: The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. What happens?

options.text: The nitrogen and the hydrogen liquefy and are then drawn off
All three gases liquefy together and are then distilled
The ammonia decomposes back to nitrogen and hydrogen
The ammonia liquefies and is removed from the gas mixture

questions.explanation: On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed, leaving the other two gases behind.

questions.stem: How does borosilicate glass differ from soda-lime glass?

options.text: It melts at a much lower temperature
It is made from pure sand and nothing else
It melts easily once it gets hot enough
It melts at a higher temperature

questions.explanation: Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.

questions.stem: Which is the usual industrial source of the hydrogen used in the Haber process?

options.text: Electrolysis of water, which splits it into elements
The air, as hydrogen is one of the gases present in it
Heating ammonia so that it splits into its elements
Natural gas, which consists mainly of methane

questions.explanation: Hydrogen is obtained from natural gas (methane) or from other hydrocarbons.

questions.stem: LD and HD poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. Why do they have different properties?

options.text: They are built from two different monomers
A different catalyst and conditions are used
HD poly(ethene) is pressed hard after it is made
The HD chains contain a second element

questions.explanation: The properties of polymers depend on the monomer and on the conditions under which they are made, so the same ethene gives two different materials.

questions.stem: Which balanced symbol equation represents the Haber process?

options.text: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ NH3
N2 + H2 ⇌ NH3

questions.explanation: Two nitrogen atoms and six hydrogen atoms appear on each side, so the equation is balanced.

questions.stem: Why do thermosetting polymers keep their shape when they are heated?

options.text: They only melt above about a thousand degrees
The covalent bonds in the chains never break
They contain no carbon that could be melted
Cross-links join the chains to each other

questions.explanation: The chains in a thermosetting polymer are joined by cross-links, so they cannot slide apart and the polymer does not melt.

questions.stem: Which equation for the Haber process is written as the specification gives it?

options.text: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ammonia
ammonia ⇌nitrogen + hydrogen
nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia
nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonium

questions.explanation: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it, with the double arrow for a reversible reaction.

questions.stem: Why is a pressure of about 200 atmospheres used rather than a far higher one?

options.text: Because a higher pressure would reduce the yield of the ammonia made
Because the iron catalyst is destroyed above 200 atmospheres
Because stronger plant, more energy and greater risk cost more
Because 200 atmospheres gives the greatest possible yield

questions.explanation: Yield would rise further, but the extra pipework, compression energy and hazard are not worth the gain.

questions.stem: The nitrogen for the Haber process is taken from the air. Which reason best explains this choice?

options.text: Nitrogen taken from the air is more reactive than nitrogen from a tank
Air is free and is about 78% nitrogen, so it is the cheapest source
Air already contains all the hydrogen that is needed for the reaction
Nitrogen from the air needs no purification before it is used

questions.explanation: Commercial conditions and raw materials are chosen for availability and cost, and air costs nothing.

questions.stem: In a Haber reactor at 200 atmospheres the rate of production is 9, 21 and 33 tonnes per hour at 350, 450 and 550 degrees C. The percentage yield at the same three temperatures is 55, 28 and 12. What do the data show?

options.text: The rate is highest at 350 degrees C, where the yield is highest
The rate rises with temperature while the yield falls
Both the rate and the yield fall at higher temperatures
The rate and the yield are both highest at 450 degrees C

questions.explanation: The rate figures rise from 9 to 33 while the yield figures fall from 55 to 12.

questions.stem: At 450 degrees C the rate of ammonia production is 12 tonnes per hour at 100 atmospheres, 24 at 200 atmospheres and 45 at 400 atmospheres. What do these data show?

options.text: The rate falls as the gases are squashed up
The rate stops rising beyond 200 atmospheres
Raising the pressure does not change the rate
Doubling the pressure roughly doubles the rate

questions.explanation: 12 to 24 and 24 to 45: each doubling of the pressure roughly doubles the rate of production.
